Gas Generation

Overview

Thermal runaway reactions can generate substantial quantities of gas.

LiionTR currently represents gas generation using an empirical reaction-yield framework in which individual thermal runaway reactions are associated with prescribed gas-species yields.

The gas subsystem converts reaction progress into molar generation rates and cumulative gas inventories. These inventories may then be used by pressure and venting models.

The current gas-generation framework is intentionally reduced-order. It does not yet calculate gas composition from chemical equilibrium.

Gas Species

A gas species in LiionTR is represented by a name and molar mass.

For species \(s\), the molar mass is

\[M_s,\]

with units of kg/mol.

The molar mass is used when converting between molar and mass quantities, particularly in compressible vent-flow calculations.

Gas Inventory

The gas inventory stores the mole amount of each species,

\[n_s,\]

where \(n_s\) is expressed in mol.

For a mixture containing \(N_s\) species, the total number of moles is

\[n_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_s n_s.\]

Total Gas Mass

The total gas mass is

\[m_{\mathrm{gas}} = \sum_s n_s M_s,\]

where \(M_s\) is the molar mass of species \(s\).

The result is expressed in kg.

Mole Fractions

The mole fraction of species \(s\) is

\[x_s = \frac{n_s}{n_{\mathrm{tot}}}.\]

The mole fractions satisfy

\[\sum_s x_s = 1\]

when the gas inventory contains a nonzero amount of gas.

Mean Molar Mass

The mole-weighted mean molar mass of the mixture is

\[\overline{M} = \sum_s x_s M_s.\]

Equivalently,

\[\overline{M} = \frac{ \sum_s n_s M_s }{ \sum_s n_s }.\]

The mean molar mass is used by the current mixture vent-flow model.

Reaction Gas Yields

The empirical gas-generation model associates each thermal runaway reaction with one or more gas-species yields.

For species \(s\), the prescribed yield is

\[Y_s,\]

with units of mol/kg of reacted material.

If a reaction represents a mass fraction \(w\) of the total cell mass and progresses at a rate

\[\frac{d\alpha}{dt},\]

then the reacted-material mass rate is

\[\frac{dm_{\mathrm{reacted}}}{dt} = m_{\mathrm{cell}} w \frac{d\alpha}{dt}.\]

The corresponding gas-generation rate is

\[\dot{n}_s = Y_s m_{\mathrm{cell}} w \frac{d\alpha}{dt}.\]

The resulting unit is mol/s.

Multiple Gas Species

One reaction may generate several gas species simultaneously.

For a reaction with species yields

\[Y_1, Y_2, \ldots, Y_m,\]

the corresponding generation-rate vector is

\[\dot{\boldsymbol{n}} = \left[ \dot{n}_1, \dot{n}_2, \ldots, \dot{n}_m \right].\]

If multiple reactions generate the same species, their contributions are added.

Gas Generation Network

The gas-generation model is coupled to a liiontr.reactions.network.ReactionNetwork.

For each reaction, the model obtains the reaction progress rate and applies the corresponding gas yields.

The total generation rate of species \(s\) is therefore

\[\dot{n}_{s,\mathrm{gen}} = \sum_i Y_{i,s} m_{\mathrm{cell}} w_i \dot{\alpha}_i,\]

where \(i\) indexes thermal runaway reactions.

Cumulative Generated Gas

For a reaction that progresses from an initial conversion \(\alpha_{i,0}\) to a current conversion \(\alpha_i\), the cumulative reacted material is proportional to

\[\Delta \alpha_i = \alpha_i - \alpha_{i,0}.\]

The cumulative quantity of species \(s\) generated by that reaction is

\[n_{i,s} = Y_{i,s} m_{\mathrm{cell}} w_i \left( \alpha_i - \alpha_{i,0} \right).\]

Summing over reactions gives

\[n_{s,\mathrm{generated}} = \sum_i n_{i,s}.\]

Closed-Cell Gas Balance

Before vent opening, generated gas remains inside the cell free volume.

For each species,

\[\frac{dn_s}{dt} = \dot{n}_{s,\mathrm{gen}}.\]

The gas inventory therefore increases according to the integrated reaction-driven gas generation.

Vented Gas Balance

After vent opening, gas can both be generated and discharged.

The species balance becomes

\[\frac{dn_s}{dt} = \dot{n}_{s,\mathrm{gen}} - \dot{n}_{s,\mathrm{vent}}.\]

The current solver treats vent opening as irreversible: once the vent opens, the system remains in the vented phase.

Coupling to Pressure

The gas inventory determines the total amount of gas in the cell free volume.

The pressure model then uses

\[n_{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_s n_s\]

together with temperature and free volume to determine internal pressure.

In the current implementation, pressure is calculated using an ideal-gas model.

The pressure formulation is described separately in the pressure-model documentation.

Coupling to Venting

The gas inventory also provides the mixture composition and mean molar mass required by the current vent-flow model.

The vent-flow model calculates a total discharge rate and distributes it among individual species according to the gas-mixture mole fractions.

This approach assumes that the vented mixture has the same composition as the well-mixed gas inventory inside the free volume.

Current Assumptions

The empirical gas-generation framework currently assumes that:

  • gas yields are prescribed directly for each reaction;

  • gas yields are constant and independent of temperature and pressure;

  • generated species are known in advance;

  • gas-phase chemical reactions are not explicitly represented;

  • equilibrium composition is not calculated;

  • condensation and phase separation are neglected;

  • the free-volume gas is spatially well mixed;

  • the gas temperature is represented by the cell temperature in the coupled thermal problem;

  • gas dissolution in electrolyte or porous materials is not represented.

Limitations of Direct Species Yields

Direct reaction-to-species yields are useful for testing, reduced-order models, and empirical fitting, but they have important limitations.

Actual lithium-ion battery thermal runaway may produce complex mixtures containing species such as hydrogen, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, water vapor, methane, ethylene, and other hydrocarbons.

The product distribution can depend on temperature, state of charge, electrode chemistry, electrolyte composition, pressure, secondary gas-phase chemistry, and material decomposition pathways.

A fixed yield model cannot generally capture these dependencies.

Future Thermochemical Architecture

A more physically general gas model may represent reaction progress in terms of elemental source inventories rather than fixed gas-species yields.

Conceptually, the future architecture may use

\[\text{reaction progress} \rightarrow \text{element inventory} \rightarrow \text{chemical equilibrium} \rightarrow \text{gas composition}.\]

The elemental inventory could include elements such as

\[\mathrm{C,\ H,\ O,\ N,\ F,\ P,\ Li},\]

depending on the modeled battery chemistry.

A thermochemical backend could then determine equilibrium species, pressure, mixture molar mass, heat capacities, and other gas properties.

Cantera is a candidate backend for this functionality.

Relationship to Cantera

The current liiontr.chemistry.cantera.CanteraBackend is only a software interface skeleton.

It does not yet replace the empirical gas-yield model.

A future Cantera-based implementation may calculate gas-phase thermodynamic and chemical-equilibrium states from reaction-derived element inventories.

This separation is intentional: the existing empirical framework provides a simple and testable gas model while the thermochemical architecture is developed independently.

Implementation

Gas species and inventories are implemented in

liiontr.gases.inventory.

Empirical reaction gas yields are implemented by

liiontr.gases.yield_model.ReactionGasYield.

Reaction-network gas generation is implemented by

liiontr.gases.generation.GasGenerationModel.

Pressure calculations are handled separately by

liiontr.gases.ideal.IdealGasPressureModel.

Gas discharge is handled by the vent-flow models in

liiontr.gases.vent.
